51.question: Which LabVIEW structure repeatedly executes the code contained inside it until a Boolean stop condition is met?

options.a: While Loop
options.b: For Loop
options.c: Case Structure
options.d: Sequence Structure

51.explanation: The While Loop repeats execution of its subdiagram indefinitely until its conditional terminal receives the Boolean value that indicates it should stop.

52.question: Which terminal of a For Loop determines the number of iterations that will be executed?

options.a: The count terminal (N)
options.b: The conditional terminal (i)
options.c: The iteration terminal (i)
options.d: The shift register

52.explanation: The For Loop's count terminal 'N', in the upper-left corner, defines how many times the loop will execute.

53.question: Which terminal, present in both the While Loop and the For Loop, indicates the current iteration number, starting at zero?

options.a: The 'i' terminal (iteration counter)
options.b: The 'N' terminal
options.c: The conditional terminal
options.d: The shift register

53.explanation: The 'i' terminal returns the index of the current iteration, starting at 0 on the first iteration and incrementing on each pass of the loop.

54.question: By default, how is the conditional terminal of a newly created While Loop configured in LabVIEW?

options.a: As 'Stop if True'
options.b: As 'Continue if True'
options.c: As 'Stop if False'
options.d: It has no default configuration and must be chosen

54.explanation: By default, a newly created While Loop uses 'Stop if True': the loop stops on the iteration where the conditional terminal receives TRUE.

55.question: If the conditional terminal of a While Loop is configured as 'Continue if True' and is wired directly to a FALSE constant, what happens?

options.a: The loop executes exactly once and then stops
options.b: The loop runs indefinitely and never stops
options.c: The VI cannot compile (broken VI)
options.d: The loop does not execute at all

55.explanation: With 'Continue if True', the loop continues as long as it receives TRUE; if the input is a FALSE constant, the stop condition is met immediately after the first iteration.

56.question: Which of the following statements about a For Loop is correct?

options.a: A For Loop always executes a predefined number of iterations, determined before loop execution begins
options.b: A For Loop can run an indefinite number of times regardless of the value of N
options.c: A For Loop can never have a conditional terminal
options.d: A For Loop does not accept input tunnels

56.explanation: The number of iterations of a For Loop is determined by the value wired to its N terminal before the loop starts executing (or by auto-indexing of an input array).

57.question: Besides the count terminal N, what other way exists in modern LabVIEW versions to determine the number of iterations of a For Loop without wiring N explicitly?

options.a: Connect an array to an input tunnel with auto-indexing enabled; the number of iterations matches the number of elements in the array
options.b: Use a shift register exclusively
options.c: Type the number directly into the loop icon
options.d: It is not possible; N must always be wired manually

57.explanation: If an array is connected to the For Loop input with auto-indexing enabled, the loop runs as many iterations as the array has elements, with no need to wire N.

58.question: A For Loop can optionally include a conditional terminal (added by right-clicking > 'Conditional Terminal'). What effect does this have?

options.a: It lets the For Loop finish before completing the N iterations if the stop condition is met
options.b: It automatically turns the For Loop into a While Loop, removing the N terminal
options.c: It makes the loop ignore the value of N entirely
options.d: It can only be used if the loop has no shift registers

58.explanation: By adding a conditional terminal to a For Loop, it can stop before reaching N iterations if the stop condition is met, combining the behavior of both loops.

59.question: A For Loop has its N terminal wired with the value 5 and, in addition, an input tunnel with auto-indexing connected to a 3-element array. How many iterations will the loop execute?

options.a: 3, because LabVIEW uses the smaller of N and the size of the indexed array
options.b: 5, because N always takes priority over the array size
options.c: 8, because LabVIEW adds both values together
options.d: The VI breaks and cannot run

59.explanation: When N and array auto-indexing determine different iteration counts, LabVIEW executes the smaller of the two values to avoid reading past the bounds of the array.

60.question: Which element must be added to a While Loop in order to stop it in a controlled way during execution?

options.a: A Boolean control wired to the conditional terminal
options.b: A numeric indicator wired to the i terminal
options.c: A mandatory shift register
options.d: A Formula Node

60.explanation: To stop a While Loop in a controlled way (for example with a 'Stop' button), a Boolean control is wired to the loop's conditional terminal.

61.question: What is a Shift Register used for in a loop (While Loop or For Loop)?

options.a: To pass the value of a variable from the end of one iteration to the start of the next
options.b: To count the total number of iterations executed
options.c: To stop the loop automatically after a given time
options.d: To convert numeric data to Boolean

61.explanation: The Shift Register makes a value calculated in one iteration available as an input in the next iteration, enabling cumulative calculations such as running totals or counters.

62.question: Where are the two halves of a Shift Register located graphically on the border of a loop?

options.a: One on the left border (input to the next iteration) and one on the right border (output value of the current iteration)
options.b: Both on the top border of the loop
options.c: Both on the bottom border of the loop
options.d: One inside the loop and one outside the block diagram

62.explanation: The right terminal of the Shift Register stores the value at the end of each iteration, and the left terminal delivers it as input at the start of the next iteration.

63.question: What value does a Shift Register take on the first iteration of a loop if no initial value is explicitly wired to the left terminal (outside the loop)?

options.a: The default value of the data type (for example 0 for numerics) or the last value from a previous run, depending on the configuration
options.b: Always a run-time error
options.c: Always the maximum representable value of the data type
options.d: A random value on each run

63.explanation: If not explicitly initialized, the Shift Register uses the data type's default value on the first run, although the recommended practice is always to initialize it explicitly to avoid dependencies on previous runs.

64.question: What is a 'Feedback Node' in LabVIEW and how does it mainly differ from a Shift Register?

options.a: It is a node that serves a similar purpose to the Shift Register (passing data between iterations) but is added automatically when you wire the output of a node back to its own input inside a loop
options.b: It is a function exclusively for error handling
options.c: It is a type of obsolete sequence structure
options.d: It is a node that only works with arrays

64.explanation: The Feedback Node appears automatically when the output of a function is connected back to its own input inside a loop, and serves a purpose equivalent to a single-stage Shift Register.

65.question: A Shift Register can be configured with multiple additional terminals on the left border (right-click > Add Element). What is this functionality for?

options.a: To access values from iterations earlier than the immediately previous one (for example, two or three iterations ago)
options.b: To automatically increase the number of loop iterations
options.c: To convert the loop into a Case Structure
options.d: To allow multiple simultaneous stop conditions

65.explanation: By adding extra terminals to the left of a Shift Register, each one stores the value from a different earlier iteration, making it possible to access, for example, the value from two iterations back.

66.question: If you need to compute a running total of the values generated on each iteration of a For Loop, which element is most appropriate for storing the accumulated value between iterations?

options.a: A Shift Register
options.b: A tunnel with auto-indexing
options.c: The N terminal
options.d: The conditional terminal

66.explanation: The Shift Register is the natural tool for maintaining and updating an accumulated value (such as a sum) across successive iterations of a loop.

67.question: Which structure executes one of several alternative subdiagrams depending on the value of a selector?

options.a: Case Structure
options.b: Sequence Structure
options.c: While Loop
options.d: Formula Node

67.explanation: The Case Structure evaluates the value wired to its selector terminal and executes only the subdiagram ('case') corresponding to that value.

68.question: Which data types can be connected to the selector of a Case Structure?

options.a: Boolean, integer, string or enum, among other discrete types
options.b: Boolean only
options.c: Arrays only
options.d: Any data type, including complete clusters

68.explanation: The selector of a Case Structure accepts discrete types such as Boolean, integer numeric, string and enum; it does not directly accept types such as arrays or complete clusters.

69.question: When the selector of a Case Structure is Boolean, how many cases does the structure have by default?

options.a: Two: True and False
options.b: Only one
options.c: Three: True, False and Default
options.d: It depends on the number of possible enum values

69.explanation: With a Boolean selector, the Case Structure automatically generates exactly two cases: True and False.

70.question: When the selector of a Case Structure is an integer (numeric) and cases have not been defined for every possible value, what is mandatory to include?

options.a: A 'Default' case that handles any value not explicitly covered
options.b: A case named 'Error', mandatorily
options.c: Nothing; LabVIEW silently ignores values not covered
options.d: An additional Shift Register

70.explanation: With numeric or string selectors, because the range of possible values is potentially unbounded, LabVIEW requires (or strongly recommends) defining a Default case for values not explicitly specified.

71.question: What happens to the subdiagrams of a Case Structure that do NOT correspond to the current selector value?

options.a: They do not execute at all during that execution of the structure
options.b: They execute in parallel with the selected case
options.c: They execute after the selected case, in the background
options.d: They generate a run-time error

71.explanation: Only the subdiagram corresponding to the value received at the selector executes; the remaining cases are neither evaluated nor executed on that pass.

72.question: What happens if an output tunnel of a Case Structure is not wired in ALL of the defined cases?

options.a: LabVIEW flags a wiring error (broken VI) until the output is wired in every case, or the 'Use Default If Unwired' option is used
options.b: LabVIEW automatically uses zero for all cases with no configuration needed
options.c: The VI runs correctly, ignoring the unwired cases
options.d: It only generates a warning, without preventing execution

72.explanation: By dataflow, each output tunnel must receive a defined value in every case; if it is missing in any of them, LabVIEW breaks the VI unless it is explicitly configured to use a default value when unwired.

73.question: When using an enum as the selector of a Case Structure, how are the different cases usually identified on the top border of the structure?

options.a: By the text names (strings) associated with each enum value
options.b: By numbers only, with no names
options.c: By colors, with no text
options.d: By mandatory custom icons

73.explanation: When the selector is an enum, the Case Structure shows on its top border the text names associated with each enum value, making the code easier to read.

74.question: Which type of selector is commonly used in a Case Structure to handle different kinds of errors centrally within a VI?

options.a: A selector based on the error cluster (using the error code or its Boolean status)
options.b: An array selector
options.c: A complete, unbundled cluster selector
options.d: A waveform selector

74.explanation: It is common to wire the Boolean status or the numeric code of an error cluster to the selector of a Case Structure, in order to run conditional error handling depending on whether an error occurred.

75.question: You have a Case Structure with an integer selector and cases defined for 0, 1, 2 and 'Default'. If at run time the selector receives the value -1, which case executes?

options.a: The Default case
options.b: A run-time error occurs and the VI stops
options.c: Case 0, because it is the closest
options.d: No case executes and the VI waits indefinitely

75.explanation: Any integer value that does not match an explicit case (including negative values) is caught by the Default case, which acts as the general handler for values not covered.
